docs.title: SlotServe
docs.text: SlotServe turns a GPU server into a shared, bookable service. People book time slots in a web calendar, get exclusive use of the GPU during their slot, and call models through an OpenAI-compatible API with their own key. SlotServe runs the model server for you - llama.cpp's llama-server, vLLM, SGLang or your own - and switches models automatically before each booking.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A lab or small team often shares a single big GPU. Without coordination people step on each other: one person's 30B model is unloaded by someone else's experiment, nobody knows who is using the card, and long model loads from spinning disks waste everyone's time. SlotServe fixes that with three rules:

  1. Bookings are exclusive. During your slot only your API keys are accepted.
  2. Idle time is shared. When nobody has booked the GPU, every key can use the default model.
  3. Switching models requires a booking. That lets the scheduler load your model before your slot starts.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Calendar booking Drag across a week view to book; first come, first served; optional admin approval OpenAI-compatible gateway /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings and any other route of the model server, with streaming Per-user API keys Create, name and revoke keys; only a SHA-256 hash is stored Managed model servers Started, health-checked, restarted and switched by SlotServe; per-model launch arguments edited in the browser Preloading Load times are learned per model; the next booking's model is loaded ahead of time Model downloads Paste a direct link (e.g. a Hugging Face resolve URL); resumable, one at a time Usage Requests, prompt/completion tokens and booked hours per person and per model Admin panel Manage users, bookings and API keys, change settings at runtime, audit log Flexible bookings Whole-GPU slots, argument presets, weekly repeats, extensions, waitlist, quotas Dev environments Book GPU time as a Docker container you SSH into: PyTorch, TensorFlow, CUDA or your own image; save it as an image for next time Multiple GPUs & engines Lanes of GPUs booked independently; llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang or custom servers; optional approval mode Integrations Notifications and a booking bot on Telegram, Feishu / Lark, DingTalk, WeCom and QQ, group webhooks, calendar feeds, CSV export, Prometheus metrics GPU status Memory, utilization, temperature and power from nvidia-smi Bilingual UI English and Simplified Chinese Simple deployment One container, SQLite, three bind mounts

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    browser["Browser"] -- "/api" --> web
    clients["OpenAI SDKs and tools"] -- "/v1 + API key" --> gw
    subgraph slotserve["SlotServe · one container · SQLite"]
        direction TB
        web["Web API<br/>bookings · models · admin"]
        gw["Gateway<br/>auth · admission · usage"]
        sched["Scheduler<br/>one per lane"]
    end
    subgraph gpus["GPU lanes"]
        direction TB
        l1["Lane 1 · GPU 0<br/>llama-server"]
        l2["Lane 2 · GPU 1,2<br/>vLLM / SGLang / custom"]
    end
    gw -- "forwards requests" --> gpus
    sched -- "start · switch · stop" --> gpus

A lane is a group of GPUs with its own model server, scheduler and calendar. A single-GPU host has exactly one lane and never shows lane controls.

  • How scheduling works - what happens around a booking.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
SlotServe exposes an OpenAI-compatible API at /v1. Any OpenAI SDK or tool that lets you set a base URL works.

Setting Value Base URL http://<server>:8000/v1 API key a key from the Access credentials page (sk-ss-...) Model the loaded model's name, or anything else (see below)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
PythoncurlEnvironment 
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://<server>:8000/v1", api_key="sk-ss-...")
stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="Qwen3-32B-Q4_K_M",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain KV caching in one paragraph."}],
    stream=True,
)
for chunk in stream:
    if chunk.choices:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="", flush=True)

curl http://<server>:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-ss-..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "Qwen3-32B-Q4_K_M", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}'

export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://<server>:8000/v1
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-ss-...

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method Path Notes GET /v1/models Models you can use right now (loaded or loading on a lane you may use) POST /v1/chat/completions Streaming supported POST /v1/completions Streaming supported POST /v1/embeddings The model must be started with --embedding POST /v1/* Any other route of the model server is forwarded under the same rules

The key can be sent as Authorization: Bearer <key> or x-api-key: <key>.

docs.title: The model field
docs.text:
Each lane serves one model at a time. The field picks the lane:

  • a model that a lane you may use is serving → that lane (your booked lane first);
  • empty or a name SlotServe does not know → your booked lane, otherwise a free lane;
  • a registered model that is only served on a lane someone else booked → 403 gpu_reserved;
  • a registered model that no lane is serving → 409 model_not_loaded. Book a slot to load it.

The request always reaches the model server with the served model's name, so engines that check the name (vLLM, SGLang) accept it. See GPUs, lanes & engines for the full routing.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Errors use the OpenAI shape: {"error": {"message", "type", "code"}}.

Status code Meaning 401 missing_api_key / invalid_api_key No key, unknown key or revoked key 403 gpu_reserved Someone else has booked the GPU (or the lane serving that model) right now; the message says until when 409 model_not_loaded You asked for a registered model that no lane you may use is serving 503 gpu_exclusive Your own whole-GPU booking is running, so no model is served 503 model_switching Running requests are finishing before a model switch; honour Retry-After 503 model_unavailable The model is loading or failed to start; honour Retry-After 502 upstream_error The model server did not answer

docs.title: Usage accounting
docs.text: Every request is logged with its user, key, model, token counts and duration. For streaming chat and completion requests SlotServe adds stream_options.include_usage = true so the final chunk carries token counts; clients see one extra chunk with an empty choices list, as with OpenAI.

docs.title: Web API
docs.text: The browser UI uses a separate JSON API under /api with cookie sessions. After 10 failed sign-ins for one account (or 30 from one address) within 15 minutes, sign-in returns 429 too_many_attempts until the window passes. Its interactive reference is served at /api/docs. Admin endpoints live under /api/admin (stats, users, keys, reservations with approve and reject, lanes, runtime (details, load history, log download and a live stream of server-sent events), requests, runtime/manual, settings, backups, audit) and require an admin session. Storage: GET/POST /api/admin/storage, PUT/DELETE /api/admin/storage/{id}, POST /api/admin/storage/{id}/check and GET /api/admin/storage/{id}/usage (passwords are write-only: has_password tells whether one is stored); GET /api/storage lists the storages of the signed-in person. The model catalog is under /api/catalog (see Model catalog).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: SlotServe reads SLOTSERVE_* environment variables, or a .env file in its working directory. Docker Compose loads .env automatically.

docs.title: Compose variables
docs.text:
These only exist in docker-compose.yml and describe the host.

Variable Default Description LLAMA_CPP_DIR required Directory containing llama-server; mounted read-only at /opt/llama.cpp MODELS_DIR required Directory with .gguf files; mounted at /models DATA_DIR ./data SQLite database and logs; mounted at /data PORT 8000 Published port CUDA_IMAGE nvidia/cuda:12.8.1-runtime-ubuntu24.04 Base image; match the CUDA major version of your llama.cpp build

docs.title: llama-server
docs.text: SlotServe runs SLOTSERVE_LLAMA_SERVER_CMD for llama.cpp models; in Docker that is /opt/llama.cpp/llama-server, the llama-server in LLAMA_CPP_DIR. The health check engine (and the setup checklist item Inference engine) says whether it is found. If not: LLAMA_CPP_DIR must be the directory that contains llama-server itself (usually llama.cpp/build/bin), the file must be executable and built for this machine, and shared builds need their lib*.so files next to it. Without Docker, set SLOTSERVE_LLAMA_SERVER_CMD to the full path.

docs.title: SlotServe settings
docs.text: Admins change every setting except the deployment parameters in Admin → System settings, without a restart: overrides live in the database and win over .env, and Use default removes one. Each change is in the audit log with its old and new value (secrets only as a fingerprint) and can be undone. Level is where the setting appears: basic on the policy cards, advanced in the full list, expert folded away. Settings marked ⚠️ can run commands as root on the host (an engine command, a mounted directory, a forwarder image): changing them is recorded as a sensitive change and announced to all admins (a later version also asks for your password again). The deployment parameters are read at start: change them in .env and restart.

docs.title: Per-model launch arguments
docs.text:
Each model has a free-form argument string that is appended to the command. For llama.cpp models:

<SLOTSERVE_LLAMA_SERVER_CMD> -m <file> --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 --alias <name> <your arguments>

vLLM, SGLang and custom engines build their command the same way; see GPUs, lanes & engines.

-m, --host, --port and --alias are always set by SlotServe; copies in your arguments are ignored. Useful arguments:

Goal Arguments Offload all layers -ngl 99 Context size -c 16384 Parallel requests -np 4 (context is split between slots) Flash attention --flash-attn on Vision models --mmproj /models/mmproj-model-f16.gguf Embeddings --embedding --pooling mean KV cache quantization -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0

Run llama-server --help for the full list. After editing the arguments of the loaded model, press Reload model on the overview page.

docs.title: Backups and restore
docs.text:
SlotServe writes a backup bundle (database, generated secret key, SSH host keys, manifest) to data/backups/ every day at SLOTSERVE_BACKUP_HOUR, keeps the newest SLOTSERVE_BACKUP_KEEP, and copies each one to SLOTSERVE_BACKUP_TARGET (a mounted path or storage:<id>) when it is set. Admin → Overview → Backups lists them and makes one on demand. A snapshot is also taken before every database upgrade; those are never deleted. slotserve restore <bundle> puts one back (with the server stopped) and the next start shows a reconciliation report.

Workspaces, kept environments' data, saved images and models are not part of a backup. Details, the off-machine copy and the restore steps: Backups and Restore from a backup.

docs.title: First admin and setup code
docs.text:
While no admin account exists, SlotServe prints a one-time setup code in its log at every start:

docker compose logs slotserve | grep -A4 "No admin account"
docker compose exec slotserve slotserve setup-code     # or ask for it directly

Open SlotServe: the sign-up form asks for the setup code instead of the invite code, and the account becomes the admin. The code stops working as soon as an admin exists, and installations that already have an admin never ask for it. Everyone else signs up with the invite code (or is created in Admin → Users).

docs.title: Requests from other pages
docs.text:
SlotServe refuses changing requests (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) to its own API that do not come from its own pages: an Origin must be SlotServe's own address (the host the browser used, or SLOTSERVE_PUBLIC_URL), Origin: null is always refused, and requests with the session cookie but without Origin must carry the header X-SlotServe: 1 (the web UI sends it). This stops pages on dev environment ports or other sites from acting for a signed-in person. API clients are not affected: /v1 with API keys, /metrics, chat platform callbacks and scripts without the session cookie.

Behind a reverse proxy, pass the original host (proxy_set_header Host $host; for nginx) or set SLOTSERVE_PUBLIC_URL; otherwise changes made in the web UI are refused with "did not come from a SlotServe page".

docs.title: Admin command line
docs.text:
Most account tasks are done in Admin → Users. The command line is for when no admin can sign in:

docker compose exec slotserve slotserve setup-code               # code for creating the first admin
docker compose exec slotserve slotserve reset-password <username>
docker compose exec slotserve slotserve set-admin <username>
docker compose exec slotserve slotserve set-admin <username> --revoke
docker compose exec slotserve slotserve doctor                   # run the health checks (exit code 1 on an error)
docker compose run --rm --no-deps slotserve slotserve restore <bundle>   # with the server stopped

See Operations for when to use which.

docs.title: Dev environments
docs.text:
A dev environment is a Docker container of your own on the server: VS Code, JupyterLab or a desktop in the browser, or a terminal over SSH. Your files in /workspace are kept between environments. Start one without a GPU at any time to write code and set things up, and book a GPU when you need it; you can keep the whole environment too. Lanes can also run a shared environment everyone who joined can log into while nobody has them booked.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as You
    participant S as SlotServe
    participant D as Docker
    U->>S: Open: VS Code (browser), no GPU
    S->>D: pull the image if needed, create a network and the container (/workspace, /models read-only)
    S-->>U: the card shows Open when it is ready (about a minute)
    U->>S: Open
    S-->>U: one-time link to the web port (:8001), VS Code opens in a new tab
    Note over U,D: later: with a GPU for a booked time
    S->>S: at the start: stop the lane's model server
    S->>D: the container gets the lane's GPUs (and SSH, when you added a key)
    Note over S,D: when the booking ends
    S->>D: remove the container (/workspace stays; a kept environment is only paused)
    S->>S: load the lane's default model again

docs.title: Your first environment: VS Code in the browser
docs.text:
1. Open Dev environments. Under Open an environment:
    • Choose a tool: VS Code (browser) (or JupyterLab, the Ubuntu desktop, a terminal, one of your kept environments or another template);
    • Do you need a GPU? Not now - recommended for setting up and writing code; you can move to a GPU any time;
    • press Open.
  2. The new environment's card shows its progress (the image is downloaded the first time). After about a minute it has an Open VS Code button: VS Code opens in a new browser tab, on /workspace.
  3. Work. Your files belong in /workspace, which is kept after the environment ends and is the same in every environment of yours. Everything else in the container (packages installed with apt or pip outside /workspace) is removed when it ends, unless you keep the environment or save it as an image (see Kept environments and Saving an environment).
  4. A terminal is inside VS Code (Terminal → New Terminal). You are root in the container, so apt install works without sudo. The shared models are at /models (read-only), and OPENAI_BASE_URL / OPENAI_API_KEY let code call SlotServe's models right away (see Inside the environment).
  5. When you are done, Stop it on its card. An environment without a GPU runs until you stop or pause it; there is no time limit.

No SSH key, no password and no booking are needed for the browser tools: you are signed in to SlotServe, and SlotServe signs you in to the app. Opening it goes through a one-time link to SlotServe's web interface port (8001), which keeps environments' pages apart from SlotServe itself (see Their own origin).

docs.title: With a GPU
docs.text:
Choose Yes, with a GPU instead of Not now, and pick a time: SlotServe books a free GPU for you (the same short booking dialog as on the Overview; Book with a GPU opens it directly). Or choose Dev environment in any booking dialog. The image is downloaded ahead of time; at the start of the booking the container starts with the lane's GPUs, and the card shows the time left, +1 h (it says why when the next hour is taken), live GPU use and End. When the booking ends the container is removed (/workspace stays) unless it is a kept environment; the reminder 10 minutes before the end has buttons to extend.

A kept environment you used without a GPU can be booked with a GPU and continues where you left it; see Without a GPU.

docs.title: From a terminal or local VS Code: SSH
docs.text:
The second way in is SSH, for your own terminal, VS Code Remote-SSH, scp or port forwarding. It needs an SSH public key (or the environment password) on SlotServe:

  1. Choose Terminal / SSH as the tool (or any other: they all have SSH). The page asks for your public key inline the first time: paste it, use the two commands it shows for your system to make one, or let the browser make a key pair (the private key is downloaded once, only the public key is sent). See Logging in.

  2. When the environment runs, its card shows the command:

    ssh -p 2201 root@server

  3. VS Code Remote-SSH: add the snippet from the card to ~/.ssh/config; each environment has its own Host alias and host key, so connect to that alias. The port can change between bookings.

  4. Anything you start yourself (TensorBoard, a demo, an API) can be opened in the browser under Ports on the card (see Ports), or with SSH port forwarding, e.g. ssh -p 2201 -L 8888:localhost:8888 root@server.

The first ssh to an environment asks to trust its host key: compare the fingerprint with the Host key on the card.

docs.title: Docker access
docs.text:
1. Mount the Docker socket into SlotServe. In docker-compose.yml uncomment

    - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock

    and run docker compose up -d. Containers need GPU access through the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, which the SlotServe container already uses. Without Docker in a container, the user running SlotServe needs access to the socket (the docker group). SLOTSERVE_DOCKER_HOST points elsewhere (another socket, tcp://).

  2. Turn on Admin → System settings → Dev environments → Dev environments. The setup checklist item Dev environments and the health check docker tick when Docker answers; if not, the check's evidence says why ("Cannot connect to the Docker daemon", permission denied on the socket).

  3. Open the ports people need in the host firewall: the web interface port (SLOTSERVE_DEVENV_WEB_PORT, default 8001, published by docker-compose.yml) for the browser tools, the SSH ports range (default 2200-2299; each running environment gets one port from it), and the Direct port range (default 2300-2399) if people may publish ports directly (see Ports). Docker publishes the SSH and direct ports itself, past ufw; see Ports and firewall.

  4. Optionally set SSH host name (what people should type after root@), CPU, memory and shared-memory limits, which image registries are allowed, whether Password logins are allowed, a Storage directory for persistent data, and the limits for kept environments.

Behind a reverse proxy, also set Web interface address (SLOTSERVE_DEVENV_WEB_URL); see Reverse proxy.

Security

Whoever controls the Docker socket controls the host. SlotServe only starts hardened containers without extra privileges (see Limits and hardening), with the lane's GPUs, the person's /workspace and the models directory read-only, but anyone with admin rights in SlotServe can now run containers on the host. Only enable dev environments on a server whose users you trust.

Podman provides a Docker-compatible API without a root daemon. Point SLOTSERVE_DOCKER_HOST at its socket (for example unix:///run/podman/podman.sock) to use it instead; GPU access then needs Podman's CDI setup.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Template Image Web interface PyTorch pytorch/pytorch:2.14.1-cuda12.6-cudnn9-devel JupyterLab + PyTorch quay.io/jupyter/pytorch-notebook:cuda12-pytorch-2.11.0 JupyterLab TensorFlow tensorflow/tensorflow:2.21.0-gpu-jupyter CUDA nvidia/cuda:12.9.2-cudnn-devel-ubuntu24.04 Ubuntu desktop linuxserver/webtop:ubuntu-xfce-388f14a2-ls7 Desktop (XFCE) VS Code codercom/code-server:4.141.0 VS Code (code-server)

The built-in templates use CUDA 12 builds, which run on a wide range of GPUs and drivers. Admins can change their images, switch them off or add shared templates.

Anyone can add their own template from any image (unless an admin turned custom images off or limited the registries), with an optional main process and environment variables. The image needs /bin/sh; SSH works in any image because SlotServe brings its own small static SSH server.

docs.title: Web interfaces
docs.text:
SlotServe opens any port of a running environment in the browser at /devenv/<session>/port/<port>/, served on the web interface port (see Their own origin). A template declares its web interfaces as a list of ports, each with a name and a kind (desktop, JupyterLab, VS Code or any other web app); while the environment runs, its card has an Open … button for each of them (new tab). Other ports, e.g. a TensorBoard you start yourself on port 6006, can be added under Ports or opened by typing /devenv/<session>/port/6006/ on the SlotServe address. Only the person who booked the environment and admins can open its ports (environments that belong to no booking are open to everyone signed in); you need to be signed in to SlotServe.

flowchart LR
    B[Browser] -- "server:8001/devenv/7/port/8888/ (environment cookie)" --> W[SlotServe web port]
    W -- "HTTP + WebSocket, token added" --> C["container slotserve-dev-7:8888"]
    subgraph N["network slotserve-devenv-7"]
        C
    end
  • Isolation: every environment runs on its own Docker network. Web ports are never published: when SlotServe runs in a container it joins the environment's network and reaches any port by container name; when it runs directly on the host, Docker binds each declared port to a random port on 127.0.0.1, and other ports are reached on the container's address in its network (on Linux hosts). The network is removed when the environment stops (a kept environment keeps its network, and its web addresses, until it is deleted), and leftovers are cleaned up after a restart. A lane's shared environment gets a network too; its web interfaces are open to everyone signed in.
  • Proxy: SlotServe forwards HTTP (streamed) and WebSockets (Jupyter kernels, VS Code, desktop streaming), keeps redirects and cookies under the environment's path and never passes its own session cookie on.
  • Token: each start gets a random token. JupyterLab is started with it (--IdentityProvider.token), the desktop uses it as its password and VS Code (code-server, --auth password) gets its SHA-256 as HASHED_PASSWORD (placeholder {token_sha256}); SlotServe signs you in on every request it trusts (a token header, or code-server's session cookie), so you never see a password page while nobody can use these apps without going through SlotServe. Opening one of these apps as a direct port bypasses that, so it has to be confirmed.
  • Base path: the main process and environment variables can use the placeholders {base_path} and {port} (the first declared port, e.g. /devenv/7/port/8888/ and 8888), {base_path_<port>} (any declared port, e.g. {base_path_6006}), {token}, {token_sha256} and {session}. Ports whose app is given its base path (Jupyter --ServerApp.base_url, the desktop's SUBFOLDER) receive the full path; for all other ports (code-server, most simple apps, ports that are not declared) SlotServe strips the prefix, so those apps should use relative links. The variables SLOTSERVE_WEB_BASE, SLOTSERVE_WEB_PORT and SLOTSERVE_WEB_TOKEN (first declared port) are set as well.
  • Keep the image's entrypoint: images such as the linuxserver desktop run their own init system. With this option SlotServe keeps the image's entrypoint and command and starts the SSH server next to it with docker exec, instead of using its own start script.

The built-ins: JupyterLab + PyTorch (JupyterLab on port 8888, files in /workspace), Ubuntu desktop (an XFCE desktop streamed to the browser, port 3000) and VS Code (code-server on port 8080, opened on /workspace; extensions come from Open VSX). SSH works in all of them as before.

Note

The desktop streams video with modern browser APIs that need a secure context: open SlotServe over HTTPS (or on localhost). Hardware-accelerated graphics in the desktop may need NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=all in the template's environment variables, depending on the host's driver setup.

docs.title: Their own origin
docs.text:
Apps in environments are written by whoever uses them. If they were served on SlotServe's own address, a page in someone's environment could use SlotServe with the rights of whoever opens it (an admin, for example). So the web interfaces are served on a port of their own (SLOTSERVE_DEVENV_WEB_PORT, default 8001): browsers treat it as a different site origin, and it never accepts SlotServe's login cookie.

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant S as SlotServe (:8000)
    participant W as Web port (:8001)
    B->>S: /devenv/7/port/8888/ (signed in)
    S->>S: may this person use environment 7?
    S-->>B: redirect to :8001 with a one-time token (valid one minute)
    B->>W: token
    W-->>B: cookie for /devenv/7/ only, redirect to the app
    B->>W: /devenv/7/port/8888/ (environment cookie)
  • The links on the environment cards (and old bookmarks of /devenv/… on SlotServe's address) go through SlotServe, which signs you in and hands you over; there is nothing to set up for users.
  • The cookie on the web port is HttpOnly, belongs to one environment's path, lasts 12 hours and is checked against the database on every request (a disabled account or a lost booking ends access at once).
  • SlotServe refuses changing requests (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) sent by pages on the web port, and the web port refuses requests from a page of one environment to another one's address.
  • Behind a reverse proxy or when the port is published on another number, set Web interface address (SLOTSERVE_DEVENV_WEB_URL, e.g. https://gpu-box:8443) and proxy that address to port 8001 with WebSockets enabled. For the way back to the sign-in, SLOTSERVE_PUBLIC_URL should be SlotServe's own address.
  • Environments share the web port's origin among themselves. When an app must be fully isolated from other environments' pages, publish it as a direct port (each host port is an origin of its own).
  • SLOTSERVE_DEVENV_WEB_PORT=0 serves web interfaces on SlotServe's own address again, as in earlier versions. Not recommended.

code-server runs with --auth password: SlotServe signs you in with its session cookie, so a request that does not come through SlotServe (another container, someone on the host) gets its login page.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
While an environment runs, its card lists its ports: the ones its template declares and any you add. For each port you see its name, the container port, how it is opened, its address with Open and Copy buttons, and whether something listens on it (SlotServe looks at the container's listening sockets; Localhost only means the app listens on 127.0.0.1 and must be told to listen on 0.0.0.0). Ports that something listens on but that are not listed yet are offered for adding with one click.

Each port is opened one of two ways, which you can switch at any time:

Mode Address Who can use it SlotServe login (default) http://server:8001/devenv/<session>/port/<port>/ You and admins, signed in to SlotServe. For web apps. Direct http://server:<host port> Anyone on the network, without SlotServe. Any app or protocol (HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC, databases, …).

Add port asks for the container port, a name and the mode. Adding, switching and removing ports never restarts the environment. Ports declared by a template (desktop, JupyterLab, VS Code, …) are behind the login unless the template sets them to direct; for those, removing means going back to the template's setting.

  • Direct ports come from the Direct port range (default 2300-2399, separate from the SSH ports). SlotServe starts a tiny forwarder container (socat, image Port forwarder image, default alpine/socat:1.8.1.1) on the environment's network that publishes the host port and passes connections to the environment. It runs only while the environment runs: it is removed when the port is removed or switched to the login, and when the environment stops or is paused. Direct ports are open to everyone who can reach the server; protect the app itself (a password, a token) if it matters.
  • Fixed numbers: a kept environment's direct port belongs to the kept environment. Its number stays while the environment is paused and is the same when it is continued; it is released when the kept environment is deleted (or removed for being unused). Any other environment's direct port belongs to its booking and is released when the booking ends.
  • Limits: admins set Direct ports per person (default 5; admins have no limit; 0 lets only admins publish ports) and can switch Direct ports off (forwarders stop, the numbers stay assigned).
  • Shared environments of idle lanes list only their template's ports; nobody can add ports to them.
  • A port that the host already uses is skipped when it is first published (the next free number is taken). If a fixed port is taken later, the card shows the problem.
  • Direct ports on the Dev environments page lists your direct ports, including those of paused kept environments, and lets you release one. Admins see everyone's with Everyone and can reclaim any: the host port goes back to the pool and the container port stays reachable behind the login.

docs.title: Saving an environment
docs.text:
Save as image stores the running container (installed packages, files outside /workspace) as a new template of yours, so the next booking starts exactly where you left off. /workspace is kept anyway and is not part of the image. The new template declares the environment's ports, including the ones you added and whether each is direct. The number of saved images per person is limited (default 3); deleting a saved template removes the image from the server.

Before saving (and before a kept environment is snapshotted) SlotServe empties what it copied in for this environment only: the environment key, the SSH host key and root's password hash; the SLOTSERVE_*, OPENAI_* and web token variables are emptied in the image, which keeps its own variables. The next start fills them in again.

docs.title: Inside the environment
docs.text:
Every new environment knows where it is and how to call a model (admins: Platform context in environments, on by default):

  • Variables: SLOTSERVE_USER, SLOTSERVE_END (the booking's end), SLOTSERVE_ENV_ID, SLOTSERVE_ENV (the template's or kept environment's name), SLOTSERVE_LANE, SLOTSERVE_GPUS, SLOTSERVE_MACHINE, SLOTSERVE_CHECKPOINT_DIR (/workspace/.checkpoints, a convention for training scripts) and OPENAI_BASE_URL. When a booking is extended, login shells see the new end (/run/slotserve/env); the container's own environment keeps the end it started with.
  • The LLM endpoint: OPENAI_BASE_URL is http://slotserve-gw:8002/v1, a small listener of SlotServe that serves only the /v1 API to the environments (not the web UI or /api). Requests go through the same keys, admission and usage records as on SlotServe's own port. A template that sets its own OPENAI_BASE_URL keeps it.
  • The environment key: a booked or CPU-only environment gets its own key (sk-ss-env-..., llm scope only, acting as you). It is written to /run/slotserve/llm-key (readable by root only) and exported as OPENAI_API_KEY in login shells, so python3 -c 'from openai import OpenAI; print(OpenAI().models.list())' works without any setup. It is never in the container's environment (docker inspect does not show it), is revoked when the environment stops and lives at most 24 hours at a time (moved on while the environment runs). Shared environments of idle lanes get no key: use your own API key there. Admins can switch keys off (Environment LLM key).
  • Login banner: SSH logins show at most three lines: the environment, its GPUs and the time left; /workspace usage; the LLM endpoint with a one-line example.

Shells that are not login shells (some web terminals) do not read /etc/profile.d; run . /etc/profile.d/slotserve-platform.sh there. Images that run as another user than root (their own entrypoint) cannot read the key file.

Where the listener is: when SlotServe runs on the host, on the address of Docker's default bridge (docker0, e.g. 172.17.0.1) - environments find it through /etc/hosts, and nothing outside the machine reaches it. When SlotServe runs in a container, on its own addresses, as slotserve-gw on each environment's network (the port is not published). SLOTSERVE_DEVENV_GATEWAY_PORT (default 8002, 0 = off) and SLOTSERVE_DEVENV_GATEWAY_HOST change it. A host firewall that drops traffic from containers to the host blocks it too. With Docker on another machine, environments get no LLM endpoint.

docs.title: Logging in: SSH keys and the environment password
docs.text:
Your credentials are on the Access credentials page (next to your API keys):

  • SSH public keys: paste the content of ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (create one with ssh-keygen -t ed25519).
  • Environment password: an SSH password for dev environments, separate from your SlotServe password. SlotServe stores only its SHA-512-crypt hash (the /etc/shadow format) and writes that hash into the container; the password itself is never stored. Each connection gets three tries.

A template with a web interface (JupyterLab, the desktop, VS Code) starts without any credentials: you use it in the browser, and SSH simply lets nobody in until you add a key. Any other template needs an SSH key, or an environment password while Password logins is on (the default). Admins can switch password logins off; then only keys work and SSH servers reject passwords. A new password reaches a running booked environment the next time it starts. Shared environments only accept keys.

Every environment has its own SSH host key; its fingerprint is shown with the environment. A kept environment keeps its key across pauses, GPU changes and snapshots. Environments created before this version get their own key the next time they start, so ssh warns about a changed host key once: remove the old line from ~/.ssh/known_hosts (ssh-keygen -R "[server]:port") and check the new fingerprint.

docs.title: Limits and hardening
docs.text:
Every container SlotServe creates goes through one last, fixed step before Docker sees it:

  • No new privileges (setuid programs such as sudo cannot gain rights) and a few capabilities dropped (NET_RAW, MKNOD, SYS_CHROOT, AUDIT_WRITE, SETFCAP; ping does not work). Templates whose image needs setuid programs (the built-in desktop: its init system) run in compatibility mode without the first rule; admins switch it per template and the template shows it.
  • Processes: at most SLOTSERVE_DEVENV_PIDS_LIMIT (default 4096), so a fork bomb stays inside its container.
  • Memory: the Memory limit setting, or - when it is 0 - the host's memory less max(4 GB, 10 %). Before this version 0 meant "no limit"; now an out-of-memory process is killed inside its container instead of taking SlotServe and everyone else with it. Admins see the limit that applies on the Dev environments information (/api/devenv, hardening).
  • Open files: 1048576. Logs: at most 5 files of 50 MB per container.
  • GPUs: exactly the lane's GPUs. A lane that names no GPUs cannot start a GPU environment (it used to get every GPU of the machine); give the lane its GPUs under Admin.
  • Never privileged, never the host's network, process or IPC namespace, never a bind of / or of the Docker socket.

Kept environments created by an older version are snapshotted and recreated once on their next start, because these settings cannot be added to an existing container.

What this means inside an environment (sudo, ping, killed jobs) and when to use compatibility mode: Container hardening and compatibility mode.

docs.title: Kept environments (projects)
docs.text:
Normally the container is removed when the booking ends and only /workspace stays. To keep everything you installed, choose Keep as new in the booking dialog and give the environment a name. When that booking ends the container is only stopped (paused). A later booking can Continue it: the same container starts again, with your current keys and password copied in.

  • If the next booking is on a lane with different GPUs, SlotServe saves the container as an image (a snapshot) and recreates it on the new GPUs, keeping its kept directories and settings. The same happens when its kept directories changed or its old SSH port is taken.
  • Kept directories: besides /workspace, a template or kept environment can list more directories to keep, e.g. /root or /opt/conda (absolute paths; system directories such as /etc, /usr, /proc or /opt/slotserve are not allowed). A new directory starts with the image's content. Changing the list takes effect the next time the container is created.
  • The Dev environments page lists your kept environments with their state (paused, running, not started yet, container missing), size and last use. You can rename them, change their kept directories and delete them; deleting removes the container and its snapshot, and optionally its kept directories. /workspace is never deleted.
  • One kept environment cannot be booked twice at the same time. Admins limit how many each person may keep (Kept environments per person, default 3) and can remove kept environments unused for a number of days (Remove unused kept environments after; 0 = never; their data stays).

docs.title: Without a GPU
docs.text:
Not everything needs a GPU. Editing code, moving data, installing packages or a CPU job can run in a dev environment without a GPU, at any time and without a booking:

  • On the Dev environments page, press Start without GPU in the Without a GPU section (or on a template or kept environment) and pick a template or one of your kept environments. It starts right away on the server's shared CPU cores, with the same SSH login, /workspace, kept directories and web interfaces as a booked environment, but no GPU.
  • It runs until you Pause it (a kept environment keeps its container) or Stop it (any other environment; /workspace stays). There is no idle timeout and no end time. Its card shows the CPU cores and memory it uses right now.
  • Admins limit how many each person may run at once (Without-GPU environments per person, default 2).

One kept environment, two modes. A kept environment can run without a GPU between its bookings. When a booking of it starts, SlotServe stops it and continues it with the booked lane's GPUs: the container is saved as a snapshot and recreated with the GPUs, so everything installed stays (as when a kept environment moves to other GPUs). When the booking ends it is paused as usual; with Continue without GPU after bookings switched on for that kept environment it goes on running without a GPU instead. You can also start it without a GPU again at any time. While a booking of it runs, it cannot be started without a GPU.

Snapshots

Each switch between the CPU and a booking's GPUs saves the container as an image layer. If a kept environment switches very often over a long time, delete it and keep a fresh one now and then (or save it as an image and start a kept environment from that), because images have a limit on the number of layers.

docs.title: Sharing the CPU fairly
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Host CPU cores
        A["Lane A: cores per GPU x its GPUs"]
        B["Lane B: cores per GPU x its GPUs"]
        P["Shared pool: all other cores"]
    end
    A --- BA["Booking / shared environment on lane A"]
    B --- BB["Booking / shared environment on lane B"]
    P --- C1["Environment without GPU"]
    P --- C2["Environment without GPU"]
  • Every GPU lane reserves CPU cores for whoever uses it: CPU cores reserved per GPU (default 8) times its number of GPUs (a lane that does not restrict its GPUs counts as one). Its booking containers and its shared idle environment run on exactly those cores (Docker cpuset), so CPU-only work cannot slow a GPU booking down. 0 reserves nothing.
  • Environments without a GPU share all other cores (the pool). They all get the same CPU weight, so an idle core can be used by anyone and a busy pool is split evenly. On top of that each has a hard limit: CPU limit without GPU (cores, default 4; 0 = the whole pool) and Memory limit without GPU (default 16 GB; 0 = the host default, see Limits).
  • Memory pool without GPU caps how much memory all environments without a GPU may claim together: when one starts, the memory limits of all running ones are added up, and a new one that would not fit is refused until another is paused. 0 = no total.
  • SlotServe reads the number of cores and the memory of the host from Docker. If there are fewer cores than the lanes want, each lane gets its share and at least one core stays in the pool. The section on the Dev environments page shows the pool and each lane's cores. Reserved cores are assigned by logical CPU number, in lane order.

Changing these settings applies to containers created afterwards; a kept container gets its new CPU placement and limits the next time it starts.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: The CPU time and memory of every environment without a GPU are read from Docker every few seconds and recorded each minute for its owner (kind "CPU-only environments"). The Usage page then shows CPU core-hours per person.

docs.title: What admins see
docs.text: The Without a GPU section lists every running environment without a GPU with its owner, state, CPU cores and memory in use, and a Pause / Stop button (logged in the audit log). Admins find the settings in Admin → System settings → Dev environments.

docs.title: Idle lanes: a shared environment
docs.text:
Admins choose per lane what runs while nobody has it booked (Admin → GPUs & lanes → When not booked):

Mode While the lane is not booked Run the default model The lane's default model is loaded (as before). Shared dev environment One container from a chosen template runs with the lane's GPUs. Everyone who joined it can log in. Nothing No model server and no container; the GPUs stay free.

The shared environment is stopped ahead of the next booking (like a model preload, or a whole-GPU booking's lead time) and starts again when the lane is idle; a model does not start loading until the shared environment has let go of the GPUs. The overview and the lanes page show what an idle lane is doing.

Inside, everyone who joined the lane's shared environment (on the Dev environments page; an SSH key is needed) has their own account (their user name in lower case, with characters other than letters, digits, _ and - replaced) and their SSH keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Password logins are off there, so no password hashes are copied into it. People who had an SSH key when SlotServe was upgraded to this version were joined to every lane. Home directories live on a volume per lane and are kept. root cannot log in. The Dev environments page shows the shared environment of each idle lane with your own command:

ssh -p 2205 alice@server

Accounts are created when the container starts and refreshed when someone joins, leaves or changes their keys (and once a minute). The image needs useradd or adduser; if it has neither the environment fails with a clear message. Only templates offered to everyone (built-in or shared by an admin) can be used.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Admins can add host directories, NFS exports and SMB shares in Admin → Storage for shared data, personal spaces (/workspace), project data and model libraries; see Storage. What follows is what happens without them.

By default persistent data lives in Docker named volumes: slotserve-workspace-u<user id> for /workspace, slotserve-project<id>-<path> for a kept environment's directories, slotserve-u<user>-t<template>-<path> for a template's kept directories and slotserve-idle-home-l<lane> for the homes of a lane's shared environment.

With Storage directory set to a directory on the Docker host (for example /srv/slotserve), bind mounts are used instead:

Data Directory /workspace <storage>/users/u<user id>/workspace A template's kept directory <storage>/users/u<user id>/t<template id>/<path> A kept environment's directory <storage>/projects/p<id>/<path> Homes of a shared environment <storage>/lanes/l<lane id>/home

The path is a path on the Docker host, not inside the SlotServe container. Missing directories are created by a short-lived helper container of SlotServe's own helper image (SLOTSERVE_STORAGE_HELPER_IMAGE, default busybox:1.37) that mounts only the parent folders it works in, so SlotServe does not need access to the directory itself. A new directory is filled from the environment's image, like a new volume: the content is copied out of the image with Docker's archive API, the image itself never runs for this.

docs.title: What admins see
docs.text:
• Dev environments with Everyone switched on lists every environment with its state, image, port and errors; Logs shows the container output.
  • A failed environment (image not found, container exited, no free port) shows the reason and can be started again with Try again. The person is notified.
  • On restart SlotServe keeps environments that are still running, stops kept environments whose booking is over and removes leftover containers and networks. Port forwarders are recreated for the environments that still run.
  • Direct ports with Everyone lists every published host port with its owner and environment; Reclaim frees one.
  • Shared environments: only admins can restart them or read their logs and errors (for example a failed account refresh).

docs.title: Development
docs.text: You do not need a GPU to work on SlotServe. tools/mock_llama_server.py imitates a model server: it accepts the core flags of llama-server, vLLM and SGLang, pretends to load for a few seconds and serves an OpenAI-compatible echo model with streaming and usage.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
backend/            FastAPI application (Python package `slotserve`)
  slotserve/api/      Web API routes (/api)
  slotserve/gateway/  OpenAI-compatible proxy (/v1)
  slotserve/runtime/  model server processes, engines, lanes, scheduler, GPU stats
  slotserve/services/ shared queries, model scanner, download queue
  tests/              pytest suite (uses the mock server)
frontend/           Vue 3 + TypeScript + Naive UI
tools/              mock model server
e2e/                Playwright end-to-end tests
docs/               this site (MkDocs Material, en + zh)

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
cd backend
python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate     # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest

Run it against the mock from the repository root with a .env like:

SLOTSERVE_INVITE_CODE=dev
SLOTSERVE_SECRET_KEY=dev
SLOTSERVE_DATA_DIR=./dev/data
SLOTSERVE_MODELS_DIR=./dev/models
SLOTSERVE_LLAMA_SERVER_CMD=backend/.venv/bin/python tools/mock_llama_server.py

mkdir -p dev/models && truncate -s 5M dev/models/demo-Q4_K_M.gguf   # any file ending in .gguf
backend/.venv/bin/slotserve

MOCK_LOAD_SECONDS (default 5) and MOCK_TOKEN_DELAY (default 0.03) tune the mock.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev        # http://localhost:5173, proxies /api and /v1 to :8000
npm run build      # type-checks and writes to backend/slotserve/static

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve
mkdocs gh-deploy   # publish to GitHub Pages

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Web API errors are {"detail": {"code": "...", "params": {...}}}; the frontend translates code (frontend/src/i18n). Add both English and Chinese strings for new codes.
  • Gateway errors follow the OpenAI error format and are in English.
  • All timestamps are stored and sent as UTC; the browser formats them in local time.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Every push to main and every pull request runs .github/workflows/ci.yml:

Job What it checks Lint ruff check and ruff format --check Backend tests pytest on Python 3.12 and 3.13 Frontend npm run typecheck and npm run build End-to-end starts SlotServe with the mock model server and drives the UI with Playwright (e2e/) Docs mkdocs build --strict Docker image builds the image and checks that /healthz answers

CodeQL scans Python and TypeScript weekly and on pull requests. Dependabot opens weekly update PRs for pip, npm, GitHub Actions and the Docker base image (CUDA major versions are not bumped automatically).

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Changes are described in changelog fragments (changes/unreleased/*.md, see changes/README.md), which tools/release_notes.py merges into CHANGELOG.md at release time. The full procedure, including the release candidate, is the release checklist.

  1. Bump the version in backend/pyproject.toml, backend/slotserve/__init__.py and frontend/package.json, and tag a release candidate: git tag v0.10.0-rc1 && git push origin v0.10.0-rc1. The workflow publishes 0.10.0-rc1 and rc (never latest) and a GitHub pre-release.
  2. After the candidate has been verified: python tools/release_notes.py release 0.10.0, commit, then git tag v0.10.0 && git push origin main v0.10.0.
  3. .github/workflows/release.yml builds and pushes ghcr.io/peleryuan/slotserve (0.10.0, 0.10, latest) and creates the GitHub release from the changelog section.

The documentation site deploys automatically when docs/ or mkdocs.yml change on main.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
A model takes minutes to load. Can SlotServe make it faster? Loading is bound by disk speed. Put frequently used models on an SSD (point MODELS_DIR at it, or symlink individual files). Linux caches recently read files in free RAM, so on a host with more RAM than the model size a second load is much faster. SlotServe hides the wait by preloading before bookings.

My client gets 503 model_unavailable. The model is loading or failed to start. The Retry-After header says roughly how long to wait. If it keeps failing, open Models → Server log to see the model server's error (often an out-of-memory error from a too large -c or a bad argument).

My client gets 409 model_not_loaded. The request named another registered model. Either omit model/use the loaded one, or book a slot with the model you want.

Can several people share the GPU at the same time? Yes, when nobody has booked it: every valid key can use the default model concurrently (raise -np in its launch arguments for more parallel slots). During a booking the GPU is exclusive.

Does it support multiple GPUs or multiple models at once? Yes. In Admin → GPUs & lanes split the GPUs into lanes; each lane runs its own model and is booked separately, so several models are loaded at once. To use several GPUs for one model, put them in one lane and pass the engine's multi-GPU flags (for llama.cpp --split-mode/--tensor-split, for vLLM --tensor-parallel-size). See GPUs, lanes & engines.

Can I use vLLM or SGLang instead of llama.cpp? Yes, per model: Models → Add model and pick the engine. The engine must be installed where SlotServe runs; Dockerfile.vllm builds an image with vLLM.

I forgot my password. Another admin resets it in Admin → Users, or on the server: docker compose exec slotserve slotserve reset-password <username>. See Forgotten admin password or locked out.

How do I put it behind HTTPS / a reverse proxy? Proxy port 8000 with the original Host header, WebSockets and buffering off, set SLOTSERVE_PUBLIC_URL, SLOTSERVE_COOKIE_SECURE=true and SLOTSERVE_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS, and give the dev environment web port (8001) an address of its own (SLOTSERVE_DEVENV_WEB_URL). The full nginx example is in Reverse proxy.

Changes in the web UI fail with "did not come from a SlotServe page". A reverse proxy rewrites the Host header. Pass the original one (proxy_set_header Host $host;) or set SLOTSERVE_PUBLIC_URL to the address people use; see Reverse proxy.

How do I back up? SlotServe writes a backup bundle every day (database, generated secret key, SSH host keys) to DATA_DIR/backups/. Set Copy backups to so a copy lands on another machine, and back up workspaces and models where they live. See Backups and Restore from a backup.

ssh says REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED. Once per environment after the upgrade to v0.10 this is expected: every environment now has its own host key. Compare the fingerprint with the Host key on the environment's card, then ssh-keygen -R "[server]:port". See Upgrade from v0.8.

sudo does not work in my dev environment. Environments run with "no new privileges"; you are root already, so leave sudo out. Images that need it can run in compatibility mode; see Container hardening.

How do I see why a model does not load? Open Admin → Runtime monitor. It shows the loading stage and progress, the live output of the model server, and for a failure the error, exit code, the last lines of output, the exact command that was run and, for errors SlotServe recognises, a diagnosis (below). Every earlier load is listed with the same details.

Where do the model server logs go? DATA_DIR/logs/llama-server.log for the first lane and llama-server-lane<N>.log for the others (rotated at 20 MB), also visible in the UI. The file name is the same for every engine.

docs.title: Diagnoses
docs.text:
When a model load, a dev environment, a storage or a health check fails, SlotServe compares the error and the last log lines with known failures. A recognised one comes with a diagnosis - the likely cause, the next steps and the log lines that matched - on the runtime monitor, the load history and the health table (Admin → Overview). The same causes and steps are listed here, so you can also search this page for an error text.

An unrecognised failure keeps its exit code and log tail: the error is usually near the end. Use Copy diagnosis on the card when you ask for help.

docs.title: The port is already in use by another program
docs.text:
Log lines like: couldn't bind HTTP server socket, address already in use, port is already allocated

  • Find and stop the program that holds the port (often a llama-server or vLLM started by hand, or an old service). Linux: ss -ltnp; Windows: netstat -ano
  • Or move SlotServe's ports away from it: SLOTSERVE_LLAMA_PORT for the model servers (each lane uses the next port), the SSH and direct port ranges for dev environments; then restart SlotServe
  • Retry the load once the port is free

docs.title: The disk is full
docs.text:
Log lines like: No space left on device, [Errno 28]

  • Free space on the disk named in the log: the models folder, the data directory or Docker's data root (docker system df; docker image prune)
  • Remove models or saved environment images that are no longer needed
  • Retry once there is enough room

docs.title: The context length does not fit into the GPU memory left for the KV cache
docs.text:
Log lines like: max seq len (...) is larger than the maximum number of tokens that can be stored in KV cache

  • Lower --max-model-len
  • Or raise --gpu-memory-utilization (up to about 0.95) when nothing else uses the GPU
  • Or use more GPUs (--tensor-parallel-size) or a smaller / more quantized model

docs.title: The GPU ran out of memory while loading the model
docs.text:
Log lines like: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory, CUDA out of memory, torch.OutOfMemoryError

  • Lower the context size (llama.cpp -c, vLLM --max-model-len): the KV cache grows with it
  • Offload fewer layers to the GPU (llama.cpp -ngl) or use a smaller quantization of the model
  • Check that nothing else uses the GPU (nvidia-smi): another model, a dev environment or a job

docs.title: The process was stopped because the machine ran out of RAM
docs.text:
Log lines like: Killed, Out of memory: Killed process, std::bad_alloc

  • Check free memory (free -h) and what else is running; dev environments and other models use RAM too
  • Use a smaller model or quantization; with llama.cpp put more layers on the GPU (-ngl) and do not use --no-mmap
  • For dev environments: set a memory limit so one container cannot take everything

docs.title: Docker cannot give the container a GPU: the NVIDIA Container Toolkit is missing or not set up
docs.text:
Log lines like: could not select device driver "nvidia" with capabilities: [[gpu]], nvidia-container-cli: initialization error

  • Install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on the Docker host, run sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker and restart Docker
  • Check that the host driver works (nvidia-smi) and test: docker run --rm --gpus all ubuntu nvidia-smi
  • Docker Desktop on Windows: use the WSL 2 backend with a current NVIDIA driver

docs.title: The engine's CUDA version does not match the GPU driver or the GPU
docs.text:
Log lines like: CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version, no kernel image is available for execution on the device

  • Update the NVIDIA driver on the host, or use an engine build for an older CUDA version
  • With Docker: the CUDA major version of CUDA_IMAGE must match the one llama-server was built with
  • A very new or very old GPU needs a build that includes its architecture (CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES)

docs.title: The engine cannot start: a library it needs (a DLL or .so) is missing
docs.text:
Log lines like: error while loading shared libraries: libcudart.so.12: cannot open shared object file

  • Usually the CUDA runtime does not match the engine build: install the matching CUDA runtime or use an engine build for the installed CUDA
  • Windows: put the cudart DLLs from the llama.cpp release next to llama-server.exe
  • Linux: ldd $(which llama-server) shows which libraries are missing

docs.title: The engine program cannot be run (not executable or built for another system)
docs.text:
Log lines like: spawn failed: [Errno 13] Permission denied, exec format error

  • Make it executable: chmod +x
  • Check that the build matches this machine (x86_64 or arm64, Linux or Windows)
  • A folder mounted with noexec cannot run programs: move the engine or remount without noexec

docs.title: The engine program was not found
docs.text:
Log lines like: spawn failed: [Errno 2] No such file or directory, command not found

  • Set the full path of the engine: SLOTSERVE_LLAMA_SERVER_CMD for llama.cpp, SLOTSERVE_VLLM_CMD for vLLM; then restart SlotServe
  • With Docker: use the image variant that contains the engine (the vLLM image for vLLM models)
  • Check that the model uses the engine you installed (Models → engine)

docs.title: SlotServe cannot reach Docker
docs.text:
Log lines like: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock, permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket

  • Check that Docker is running on the host (docker info)
  • In Docker: mount the socket into SlotServe (-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock); outside Docker: the user running SlotServe needs access to it (docker group)
  • Check SLOTSERVE_DOCKER_HOST if Docker listens elsewhere (e.g. Podman's socket or tcp://)

docs.title: The Docker image could not be downloaded
docs.text:
Log lines like: pull access denied for ..., manifest unknown, toomanyrequests

  • Check the image name and tag (typos, a tag that does not exist)
  • Check that the Docker host can reach the registry (proxy, firewall, a registry mirror in /etc/docker/daemon.json)
  • Private images or Docker Hub's rate limit: docker login on the host, or pull the image once by hand (docker pull)

docs.title: The Docker host cannot mount this NFS/SMB share: the mount helper is missing
docs.text:
Log lines like: you might need a /sbin/mount.<type> helper program, wrong fs type, bad option, bad superblock

  • Install the helper on the Docker host (not in the container): nfs-common (Debian/Ubuntu) or nfs-utils (RHEL) for NFS, cifs-utils for SMB
  • Then click Check on the storage again
  • Docker Desktop: the mount happens in its VM; use a host directory storage instead

docs.title: The storage server refused the mount (wrong credentials or not allowed)
docs.text:
Log lines like: mount.nfs: access denied by server while mounting ..., mount error(13): Permission denied

  • SMB: check user name, password and domain in the storage settings
  • NFS: check that the export allows this Docker host's IP address (/etc/exports on the server, then exportfs -ra)
  • Then click Check on the storage again

docs.title: The NFS/SMB share could not be mounted: the server is not reachable or the share does not exist
docs.text:
Log lines like: mount.nfs: Connection timed out, failed to mount local volume

  • Check the server address and the share path in the storage settings
  • Check that the Docker host reaches the server (ping; NFS port 2049, SMB port 445 open)
  • Then click Check on the storage again

docs.title: Hugging Face refused access to the model
docs.text:
Log lines like: Access to model ... is restricted, 401 Client Error: Unauthorized for url: https://huggingface.co/...

  • Gated models: accept the license on the model's Hugging Face page with your account
  • Set a Hugging Face access token (SLOTSERVE_HF_TOKEN, read permission) and retry
  • Check the repository name (private or renamed repositories also answer 401/404)

docs.title: No permission to read the model files
docs.text:
Log lines like: failed to open GGUF file '...' (Permission denied), [Errno 13] Permission denied: '...'

  • Give the user that runs SlotServe and the engine read access to the models folder: chmod -R a+rX
  • In Docker the container user must be able to read it; on NFS/SMB check the uid/gid mapping and mount options (uid=, file_mode=)
  • SELinux hosts: mount the folder with :z, or check the audit log

docs.title: The model file is damaged or incomplete
docs.text:
Log lines like: invalid magic characters, failed to read tensor info, data is not within the file bounds

  • Download the model again: an interrupted download is the usual cause (compare size or SHA-256 with the source)
  • Split models (…-00001-of-00003.gguf): all parts must be there; load the first part
  • Check that the file really is a GGUF model for llama.cpp (not a safetensors file renamed)

docs.title: This engine version does not support the model's format or architecture
docs.text:
Log lines like: unknown model architecture: '...', Model architectures ['...'] are not supported

  • Update the engine: new model architectures need a recent llama.cpp release or vLLM version
  • Or use another build of the model (another quantization, or the GGUF from a different publisher)
  • llama.cpp loads GGUF files; vLLM loads Hugging Face model folders (safetensors)

docs.title: The model file is missing or cannot be opened
docs.text:
Log lines like: failed to open GGUF file '...', does not appear to have a file named config.json

  • Check that the file still exists (it may have been moved, renamed or deleted) and scan the models folder again
  • Models on NFS/SMB: check that the share is mounted on this machine
  • vLLM: the folder must contain config.json and the weights

docs.title: The model did not finish loading in time
docs.text:
Log lines like: model did not become ready within ...s

  • Large models on slow disks or network storage take longer: raise SLOTSERVE_LOAD_TIMEOUT_SECONDS
  • Look at the end of the log: a server that hangs without progress usually has another error there
  • Copy the model to a local SSD for faster loading

docs.title: A file or folder that is needed does not exist
docs.text:
Log lines like: No such file or directory, The system cannot find the file specified

  • Check the path in the log: typos in launch arguments, moved model files or a folder that is not mounted
  • Paths inside Docker differ from the host: use the path as the container sees it
  • Retry after fixing the path

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
SlotServe ships as one Docker image. It does not bundle llama.cpp: you mount the llama-server you already built for your GPU, so SlotServe works with any CUDA architecture and llama.cpp version.

Installing takes four steps on the command line. After that you only follow the setup checklist in the web UI: it ticks itself as things start working and says what is next.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Linux host with an NVIDIA GPU and driver
  • Docker with Compose v2
  • NVIDIA Container Toolkit
  • A CUDA build of llama.cpp (llama-server), or vLLM / SGLang - see GPUs, lanes & engines

Match the CUDA version

The CUDA major version of SlotServe's CUDA_IMAGE must match the one your llama-server was built with, and that CUDA version must support your GPU. See Configuration.

docs.title: 1. Build llama.cpp (skip if you already have it)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
cd llama.cpp
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON
cmake --build build --config Release -j --target llama-server
ls build/bin/llama-server

The directory that contains llama-server (and its lib*.so files for shared builds) is what you mount into the container - usually llama.cpp/build/bin.

docs.title: 2. Configure
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/PelerYuan/slotserve
cd slotserve
cp .env.example .env

Edit .env. The important values:

Variable Example Meaning LLAMA_CPP_DIR /opt/llama.cpp/build/bin Host directory with llama-server MODELS_DIR /mnt/ssd/models Host directory with .gguf files (prefer an SSD); must be readable by the container DATA_DIR ./data Database, logs, backups and the generated secret key PORT 8000 Web UI and API port SLOTSERVE_INVITE_CODE your secret Needed to sign up (until it is set, only the first admin can sign up); invite links work without it SLOTSERVE_SECRET_KEY empty Leave it empty: SlotServe generates one and keeps it in DATA_DIR/secret_key (see The secret key)

Behind a reverse proxy also set SLOTSERVE_PUBLIC_URL and read Reverse proxy. See Configuration for everything else.

docs.title: 3. Start
docs.text:
If llama.cpp currently runs as a systemd service, stop it first so the two do not compete for GPU memory:

sudo systemctl disable --now llama-server.service   # use your unit's name

Then:

docker compose pull          # the published image; or: docker compose up -d --build
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f

Prebuilt image or your own build

The published image uses CUDA 12.8 runtime libraries, which work with llama.cpp builds for any CUDA 12.x. docker-compose.yml follows a minor version (ghcr.io/peleryuan/slotserve:0.10), so docker compose pull brings fixes but never a new minor. Build locally (docker compose up -d --build) when your llama.cpp needs another CUDA major.

Open http://<server>:8000. If people should reach it from other machines, open the ports in Ports and firewall.

docs.title: 4. Create the admin account
docs.text:
The first account needs a one-time setup code, printed in the log while no admin exists:

docker compose logs slotserve | grep -A4 "No admin account"
docker compose exec slotserve slotserve setup-code          # or ask for it directly

On the sign-up form enter the setup code; that account becomes the admin, and the code stops working. See First admin and setup code.

docs.title: 5. Follow the setup checklist
docs.text:
After signing in, the Overview starts with Finish setting up SlotServe, and Admin → Overview shows the full Setup progress. Each item ticks itself when the thing really works (not when a form was filled in), and nothing in it blocks SlotServe from being used:

Item Ticks when How Inference engine llama-server (or your engine) is found Check LLAMA_CPP_DIR in .env; for vLLM see GPUs, lanes & engines. GPUs nvidia-smi sees your GPUs The NVIDIA Container Toolkit; GPUs gone if not. With several GPUs, decide how to split them into lanes in Admin → GPUs & lanes. A model and an idle default A model is registered and every lane has a default model Models → Scan folder registers every .gguf in MODELS_DIR (or deploy one from the Model catalog), then Set as default. The default model serves everyone while the GPU is not booked. Invite people The invite code is set (or you dismiss the item because you only hand out invite links) Create invite link: it expires, counts its sign-ups, can be revoked and comes with a ready-to-post message (Admin → Users). Or set Invite code in Admin → System settings. Optional: Dev environments Docker is reachable and dev environments are on Mount the Docker socket and switch them on: Dev environments. Optional: Chat notifications A chat platform is connected Notifications & integrations. Without one, everything still lands in the inbox. Optional: Backups kept elsewhere A backup was copied off the machine Set Copy backups to: Backups.

Below the checklist, the System health table lists every check SlotServe runs, with buttons and a diagnosis when something fails; Health checks explains each.

docs.title: 6. Three things to try
docs.text: Everyone who signs in for the first time sees Start here on the Overview with the same three paths. Try them yourself before you invite people.

docs.title: Call a model in the Playground
docs.text:
Press Try it here on the Overview (or open a model on Models). The Playground chats with a model that is already running, signed in, without an API key; next to it is the same request as Python, cURL and JavaScript. Copy code to run locally creates a key named playground (valid 90 days) on request and fills it into the code:

curl http://<server>:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-ss-..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}'

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with http://<server>:8000/v1 and a key from Access credentials. The badge next to a model says whether it is callable now, available after booking or in use by someone.

docs.title: Open VS Code in the browser
docs.text: Needs dev environments switched on (checklist item above). On Dev environments: choose VS Code (browser), answer Do you need a GPU? with Not now, press Open. About a minute later VS Code opens in a new tab, on your /workspace, which is kept after you close it. No SSH key and no booking needed; the environment runs on the CPU cores no GPU lane reserves. See Dev environments.

docs.title: Book a GPU
docs.text: Book the GPU on the Overview (or Book a slot, Schedule → New booking) opens a short dialog: what (a model, a dev environment with the GPU, or the whole GPU for your own processes), when (Now · 1 h, until a time, or a time later) - and SlotServe picks a free GPU. If it cannot be booked, the dialog says why (quota, who has it) and offers the next free time. During the booking the GPU is yours alone; see the User guide.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
git pull
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d     # or: docker compose up -d --build

Before it changes the database, SlotServe saves a snapshot in DATA_DIR/backups/ and upgrades all or nothing. Read the release's breaking changes first; for v0.8 → v0.10 follow Upgrade from v0.8.

docs.title: Running without Docker
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install ./backend
(cd frontend && npm ci && npm run build)      # outputs into backend/slotserve/static

export SLOTSERVE_LLAMA_SERVER_CMD=/opt/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server
export SLOTSERVE_MODELS_DIR=/mnt/ssd/models
export SLOTSERVE_STATIC_DIR=$PWD/backend/slotserve/static
slotserve

A systemd unit for SlotServe itself:

[Unit]
Description=SlotServe
After=network-online.target

[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/opt/slotserve
EnvironmentFile=/opt/slotserve/.env
ExecStart=/opt/slotserve/.venv/bin/slotserve
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

The admin commands (slotserve setup-code, reset-password, doctor, restore) are then run directly, as the same user and with the same environment.

docs.title: Lanes
docs.text:
A lane is a group of GPUs with its own model server process, its own scheduler and its own booking calendar. On first start SlotServe creates one lane containing every GPU that nvidia-smi reports, so a single-GPU machine needs no setup at all and shows no lane controls.

With several GPUs you decide how to split them in Admin → GPUs & lanes:

Layout Lanes Good for One big GPU GPU 0,1,2,3 Models that need all memory (tensor parallel) One lane per GPU GPU 0, GPU 1, … Several people working at the same time Mixed GPU 0+1, GPU 2, GPU 3 One large model plus smaller ones

Rules:

  • A GPU belongs to at most one lane. Changing a lane's GPUs restarts its process.
  • Each lane has its own default model, served to everyone while the lane is not booked. Instead, a lane can run a shared dev environment or nothing while idle.
  • Arguments edits the launch arguments of the model a lane is running and reloads every lane running it; Reload restarts a lane's model server. Arguments belong to the model, so they apply on every lane.
  • Bookings, waitlist entries, manual load/unload and the "fall back to the default model" behaviour are per lane. Quotas count bookings across all lanes.
  • A lane with bookings that have not ended cannot be deleted, and the last lane cannot be deleted.
  • Each lane's process gets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set to its GPUs and listens on SLOTSERVE_LLAMA_PORT + lane id - 1. Logs are per lane (llama-server-lane<N>.log).

docs.title: Which lane serves an API request
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    req(["Request with a valid API key"]) --> named{"Names a model?"}
    named -- "Yes" --> usable{"Served on a lane you may use?<br/>your booked lane first, then free lanes"}
    usable -- "Yes" --> that["That lane"]
    usable -- "No" --> taken{"Served on a lane<br/>someone else booked?"}
    taken -- "Yes" --> r403["403 gpu_reserved"]
    taken -- "No" --> known{"A registered model?"}
    known -- "Yes" --> r409["409 model_not_loaded"]
    known -- "No, unknown name" --> mine
    named -- "No" --> mine{"You have a running booking?"}
    mine -- "Yes" --> own["Your lane"]
    mine -- "No" --> ready{"A free lane with<br/>a ready model?"}
    ready -- "Yes" --> first["The first such lane"]
    ready -- "No" --> anyfree{"Any free lane?"}
    anyfree -- "Yes" --> wait["The first free lane<br/>503 + Retry-After until ready"]
    anyfree -- "No" --> r403b["403 gpu_reserved"]

In words:

  1. If the request names a model, it goes to a lane the caller may use (free, or booked by the caller) that serves that model - the caller's own lane first. A model served only on a lane someone else has booked returns 403 gpu_reserved; a registered model that no usable lane serves returns 409 model_not_loaded.
  2. Without a model name, the caller's own booked lane is used; otherwise the first free lane whose model is ready.
  3. /v1/models lists every model the caller can use right now.

docs.title: Engines
docs.text:
Each model has an inference engine. Scheduling, booking and the gateway work the same for all of them.

Engine Model source Command SlotServe runs Ready when llama.cpp (default) .gguf file llama-server -m <file> --host --port --alias <name> <args> /health returns 200 vLLM repository id or directory vllm serve <model> --host --port --served-model-name <name> <args> /health returns 200 SGLang repository id or directory python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path <model> --host --port --served-model-name <name> <args> /health returns 200 Custom anything your template, e.g. my-server --model {model} --port {port} the configured health path returns 200
  • Add models with Models → Add model. Scanned and downloaded .gguf files are llama.cpp models automatically.
  • The engine commands are admin settings (Admin → System settings → Inference engines). The command must be available where SlotServe runs.
  • Flags SlotServe sets itself (host, port, model, served name) are removed from your arguments. For tensor parallelism across a multi-GPU lane add, for example, --tensor-parallel-size 2 (vLLM) or --tp 2 (SGLang).
  • The gateway always sends the served model name upstream, so clients may omit model.

docs.title: Who may set which arguments
docs.text:
Model servers run with SlotServe's own permissions, so some flags amount to running code or writing files on the server (--trust-remote-code, plugin and module flags, anything ending in -file, -path or -dir, --log*, --ssl*, --api-key…).

  • Members may use each engine's tuning flags (context size, GPU layers, parallelism, batching, cache types, sampling defaults…) and point models at the models folder, a model library or a Hugging Face repository id. File flags such as --mmproj must name a file in the models folder or a library.
  • Other flags are refused, or, if the member chooses Ask an admin, saved as a request: the model keeps its current arguments until an admin approves it on Models (admins are notified). Presets have no requests: ask an admin to set them.
  • Admins may set anything; the flags listed above need an explicit confirmation first. Every change is in the audit log (model.args_update).
  • The custom engine is admin-only. Catalog one-click deploys only generate allowed flags.

docs.title: vLLM in Docker
docs.text:
The default image contains Python and the SlotServe server only; llama.cpp is mounted from the host. For vLLM, build the variant based on the official vLLM image:

docker build -f Dockerfile.vllm -t slotserve-vllm .
echo "SLOTSERVE_IMAGE=slotserve-vllm" >> .env
docker compose up -d

Pin VLLM_IMAGE (a build argument) to a vLLM version that supports your GPU and driver. llama.cpp can still be mounted as usual, so both engines are available.

docs.title: Approval mode
docs.text:
Admin → System settings → Accounts → Approval decides whether bookings need an admin:

Mode Needs approval Off (default) nothing Long bookings bookings longer than Approval needed above (default 4 hours) All bookings every booking

Admins' own bookings, and bookings an admin makes for someone, never need approval. A pending booking holds its time (nobody else can book it) and counts towards quotas, but no model is loaded for it. Admins approve or reject in Admin → Bookings → Awaiting approval or with the buttons in the chat message (Telegram, Feishu / Lark) or its numbered choices (DingTalk, WeCom, QQ); a weekly series can be handled at once. Requests still pending when they would start expire automatically and free their time for the waitlist.

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> pending: needs approval
    [*] --> booked: no approval needed
    pending --> booked: approved
    pending --> rejected: rejected
    pending --> expired: start time passed
    pending --> cancelled: withdrawn
    booked --> cancelled: cancelled before start
    booked --> [*]: slot ends or ended early

docs.title: Notifications & integrations
docs.text: SlotServe can message people and answer commands on Telegram, Feishu / Lark, DingTalk, WeCom and QQ, post alerts and announcements to group chats, publish bookings as calendar feeds, export usage as CSV and expose Prometheus metrics.
